identification.basis: The dictionary gives jimal 'fire stick' and jimal damal 'to make fire with a fire stick'. Roth (1904) recorded the Bloomfield River Koko-yellanji name for fire-sticks as tchi-mal, an older English-based spelling of the same word.

summary: The **[jimal](word:jimal)** is the fire drill: two sticks, one twirled upright between the palms against the other until the wood dust smoulders and lights a pinch of tinder [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904]. Roth recorded it on the Bloomfield River as *tchi-mal* (his 1904 spelling). He noted that there, unusually, women could carry fire-sticks on hunting trips [ref:roth1904]. Once fire, **[baya](word:baya)** or **[kunjin](word:kunjin)**, was made, it was kept going with a smouldering log, **[miyilkura](word:miyilkura)**, and fed with chips, **[jirramar](word:jirramar)** [ref:hershberger1982]. It was used for cooking, light and warmth, and set across the country to [hunt](entry:hunting-with-fire) and to keep the land in good order [ref:roth1901] [ref:newsport].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
**[Jimal](word:jimal)** is the fire stick. **[Jimal damal](word:jimal damal)** is 'to make fire with a fire stick', and **[dama-murnil](word:dama-murnil)** is 'twirl a fire drill' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth wrote the Bloomfield name as *tchi-mal* and the Butcher's Hill name as *mannimbal* (his 1904 spellings) [ref:roth1904].

Fire itself is **[baya](word:baya)**, which also means flame and firewood, or **[kunjin](word:kunjin)** [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary has a full set of words for a fire's life: **[jirramar](word:jirramar)**, chips and small sticks to start it; **[dalngarri](word:dalngarri)**, flames which make light; **[ngunjil](word:ngunjil)**, charcoal, hot coals or hot ashes; **[kubu](word:kubu)**, smoke; **[nulu](word:nulu)**, ashes; **[miyilkura](word:miyilkura)**, a smouldering log; and **[nyunil](word:nyunil)**, to put a fire out [ref:hershberger1982]. Out on the land, **[ngalku](word:ngalku)** is a bush fire and **[duli](word:duli)** a burnt patch of grass [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
Roth described two kinds of fire drill in North Queensland [ref:roth1904].

**The long pair.** Across the Peninsula and the far west, both sticks are thin wands of the same wood, two to four or more feet long. In the Peninsula they were kept, not thrown away, and their working ends were protected by a cap. On the Batavia, Pennefather and Embley rivers the cap was a piece of [pandanus](entry:pandanus) leaf bound with [twine](entry:string-and-twine) and sealed with warmed [beeswax](entry:native-bees) [ref:roth1904].

**The short, unlike pair.** From below the Endeavour River south to the Herbert, with its hinterland, the two sticks differ. The upright drill is a thin wand up to 15 inches long. The hearth is a flattened oval piece 8 to 12 inches long. For carrying, the pair was wrapped parcel-fashion in [paperbark](entry:paperbark) and kept in a man's [dilly-bag](entry:dilly-bags) [ref:roth1904]. The Bloomfield lies inside this area.

The drill's hearth slowly wears a round, blackened hollow. An old hollow could be used again and again until it burnt right through [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Where the materials come from
sections.body:
Fire-sticks were usually named after the timber they were made of [ref:roth1904]. The woods Roth lists, with the district for each:

- **[Grass-tree](entry:grass-tree)** (*Xanthorrhoea*): 'the most common of all, and utilised wherever available' [ref:roth1904]. Kuku Yalanji **[nganjirr](word:nganjirr)** is the grass tree [ref:hershberger1982].
- ***Premna dallachyana***: from the Endeavour River north to Princess Charlotte Bay. Said to stand up to the [wet season](entry:seasons) much better than grass-tree sticks [ref:roth1904].
- **Cotton-tree** (*Hibiscus tiliaceus*) for the drill, and *Mollinedia*, *Cryptocarya murrayi* or a split length of [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) for the hearth, on the lower Tully River [ref:roth1904].
- ***Clerodendrum inerme*** (Roth's *Clerodendron inerme*): Pennefather River, on the west coast of Cape York [ref:roth1904]. His plant list also marks it 'timber for firesticks' [ref:roth1901].
- ***Erythrina vespertilio*** (bat's-wing coral tree): 'timber for firesticks', Pennefather River [ref:roth1901].

For tinder Roth lists fine dried grass, pith dust and bits of the prickly tops of the grass-tree [ref:roth1904]. With grass-tree used 'wherever available', the drill was as much a tool of the dry inland country as of the coast [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Carrying fire.** Fire was carried as much as made. On the Keppel Islands, people carried [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) sticks alight because they smouldered slowly and saved making a new fire. Roth found that women never carried the fire-sticks, with one exception. On the Bloomfield in the old days, women might carry them on hunting expeditions [ref:roth1904]. A **[miyilkura](word:miyilkura)**, smouldering log, kept a camp fire alive [ref:hershberger1982].

**Cooking, light and warmth.** Kuku Yalanji **[jakalambal](word:jakalambal)** means both 'start a fire' and 'start to cook food' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[Jidi](word:jidi)** is a torch of [paperbark](entry:paperbark) [ref:hershberger1982]. See the [earth-oven](entry:earth-oven) entry for cooking.

**Fire on the land.** Fire was a [hunting tool](entry:hunting-with-fire). At Cape Bedford, among the Guugu Yimithirr neighbours north of Kuku Yalanji country, the whole camp would light a line of bush fires up to a mile long, running up a hill if possible. The men then spread out in a line and speared the [kangaroos](entry:wallaby) caught between them and the fire [ref:roth1901]. Roth also quotes Cook on the Endeavour River: the people could be traced 'by the fires which they kindled in their way' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: How fire was made with the drill
sections.body:
From Roth's account of twirling, which opens with Captain Cook's description from the Endeavour River [ref:roth1904]:

1. **Choose dry, soft wood.** Shape the upright stick, about 8 or 9 inches long in Cook's account, to a blunt point at one end. The hearth piece is flat.
2. **Start a hollow.** Punch a small hollow near the edge of the hearth with a sharp [stone](entry:stone) so the drill will not slip off. A split length of [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) or [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) gives a ready flat surface. An old hollow can be used again until it burns through.
3. **Prime a new hollow** with a little charcoal dust (**[ngunjil](word:ngunjil)**).
4. **Lay the tinder.** Pile a pinch of fine dry grass, pith dust or prickly grass-tree tops on a leaf or the ground, touching the edge of the hollow. On a windy day, cut a small nick from the hollow to the edge of the hearth to lead the hot dust onto the tinder.
5. **Twirl** (**[dama-murnil](word:dama-murnil)**). Hold the drill upright between the flats of both hands and spin it fast, pressing down hard. Keep shifting your hands up and running them down the stick to keep up the pressure. Cook says people got fire this way 'in less than two minutes'.
6. **Watch the dust.** The fine wood dust gathers in a little heap at the mouth of the hollow. It heats, blackens and smokes until a spark forms in it and touches the tinder.
7. **Bring it to flame.** Whip the tinder up in a bunch of dry grass, swing it round in the air and blow on it until it bursts into flame.
8. **Build the fire.** Feed it with **[jirramar](word:jirramar)**, chips and small sticks, then **[baya](word:baya)**, firewood [ref:hershberger1982].
9. **Keep it.** Bank the coals, keep a smouldering log going, or carry a glowing grass-tree stick to the next camp [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904].

The only other method Roth knew in Queensland, sawing one stick across another, he saw only on the upper Georgina River in the far west [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
Fire burns and spreads. Make fire on bare ground, away from dry grass, with water at hand. Never leave a fire unattended. [Grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) tops and dry tinder flare suddenly. Hard twirling raises blisters, so toughen your hands gradually.

Do not burn or roast **[jinjay](word:jinjay)**, the poison nut. The dictionary warns that its smoke is poisonous when the nut is roasted [ref:hershberger1982]. Smoke from any wood is hard on the lungs in a closed shelter.

Outside the small-fire allowance, lighting a fire without a permit is against the law in Queensland, and no fire may be lit during a fire ban [ref:qfd]. In national parks, camp fires are allowed only in QPWS fireplaces, fire rings or existing fire sites. Firewood must not be collected [ref:parks].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Lighting fires outdoors in Queensland is controlled by the *Fire Services Act 1990*. Fires smaller than 2 metres in any dimension may be lit without a permit if adequate precautions are taken. All other fires need a **Permit to Light Fire** from the local Fire Warden, which is free [ref:qfd]. Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* protects native title holders' hunting, gathering, fishing and cultural or spiritual activities from licence and permit requirements when done for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs [ref:alrc]. Visitors need the Traditional Owners' permission, and the landholder's on a station, before lighting any fire.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: The dictionary records that the mountain lizard **[jimalili](word:jimalili)** taught people how to use the firestick [ref:hershberger1982]. Other words: **[jirra-kangal](word:jirra-kangal)** 'to start a fire'; **[waju-l](word:waju-l)** 'to cook, burn, or light (a fire)'; **[wula](word:wula)** 'flames' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: On the Hann, fire is the great subject of the Kuku Thaypan Elders, whose knowledge of when and how to burn each kind of country is written down in Standley's 2019 thesis [ref:standley2019]. The fire-stick woods of Roth's records are here or close by: the [grass tree](entry:grass-tree) is in the Atlas for this country, and Roth's *Premna* fire-sticks were used 'From the Endeavour River up to Princess Charlotte Bay' [ref:ala-hann-fire] [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Fire-stick woods here
sections.body:
- **Grass tree**: the Atlas of Living Australia holds 14 records of *Xanthorrhoea johnsonii*, 1968–2024, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann-fire].
- ***Premna dallachyana***: fire-sticks of this wood 'are said to withstand the moisture of the wet season far better than the ordinary "grass-tree" ones'; Roth gives the Koko-rarmul name of Princess Charlotte Bay as *mo-yil* [ref:roth1904].
- **Firewood**: the Kuku Thaypan Elders say boxwood (*Ku ronga*) 'burns hot and makes good coals for fire and cooking' [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Fire's year here
sections.body:
The wet runs from December to March; by October 'the land is brown and parched' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. At Musgrave almost all of the 1174 mm of rain falls from November to April [ref:bom-musgrave]. The Elders time each burn by the country's own signs [ref:standley2019]:

- Gum-tree country 'is ready for burning when the Ku akalmba Messmate is flowering', and 'The last of the light squally showers and the SE knock em down rain is an indicator for this system, when Eriachne sp is setting seed and bark has shed'.
- In boxwood country, 'protect developing boxwood flowers through cool burns in the early dry season'.

sections.heading: How fire was used here
sections.body:
**Burning by hand (Kuku Thaypan).** The Elders light from single points: 'Single ignition points generate elliptical burns, which are naturally cooler than a linear fire'. 'A bark torch may also be used to carry fire as you spread ignition points apart', and the fire is set against the wind so that it 'burns back on itself, moves slowly and is less intense' [ref:standley2019]. This care protects food: one photograph shows 'a cool fire that has burnt the dead grass around the yams, enabling them room to spread' [ref:standley2019]. A Thaypan man told the Federal Court of looking after his country 'including through burning' [ref:fca-thaypan].

**The fire bird.** The old people said of the brown falcon: 'He picks up a burning stick from the fire, fly's away and drops it to make his own fire for hunting' [ref:standley2019].

**A story.** Roth printed a Koko-warra story from Princess Charlotte Bay, set on a lake of the old Lakefield Station, about fire-sticks, a wagtail and an owl [ref:roth1903]. It belongs to its custodians and is not retold here.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The Possum and Thaypan determinations of November 2023 recognise the right to 'light fires on the area for cultural, spiritual or domestic purposes including cooking, but not for the purpose of hunting or clearing vegetation' [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. In Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park, 'Most of the vegetation on Rinyirru is fire-dependent' and planned burns are part of its management [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]. Campers may light open fires only in fire rings, and not during fire bans, and must not collect firewood in the park [ref:qpws-hann-crossing]. Outside the park the general fire-permit rules above apply [ref:qfd].

locations.summary: On the Western Yalanji Mitchell, Roth's only fire-stick record is E. Palmer's, of a *Psychotria* wood [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Fire-stick woods here
sections.body: ***Psychotria*** species: on the Mitchell River, the river of Western Yalanji country, from E. Palmer's report [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: On Western Yalanji country, the 2026 determination recognises rights to access and camp on Country, alongside pastoral and mining interests [ref:nit2026].

locations.summary: On the Eastern Kuku Yalanji coast, cultural burning is being brought back by the Traditional Owners and their rangers [ref:newsport] [ref:ekyrangers].

sections.heading: Fire on the land here
sections.body:
Eastern Kuku Yalanji people used cultural burning to keep the land healthy for thousands of years before colonisation [ref:newsport].

**Working wood.** Charring in the fire hardened digging sticks and fighting poles. Red-hot cinders were laid in a hollow and blown on to burn out the socket of a [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) or the bowl of a dug-out water-carrier [ref:roth1904]. The wattle turtle-spear point **[kurrajan](word:kurrajan)** was put in the fire until it was hard enough to pierce a turtle shell [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
On the Eastern Kuku Yalanji Indigenous Protected Area and the Daintree-area national parks, the Eastern Kuku Yalanji rangers carry out the Jabalbina Fire Management Plan with QPWS and Queensland Rural Fires [ref:ekyrangers].

On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, the national parks handed back in 2021 are jointly managed with the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [ref:nit2021]. Jabalbina Yalanji Aboriginal Corporation and the Wet Tropics Management Authority are setting up a cultural burning project, *Return to Country Bama on Bubu*. It combines Traditional Owner knowledge with fire science to reduce bushfire risk, restore fire-dependent ecosystems and support cultural stewardship [ref:newsport].
